decision_semantics.approved: Approve suggestion for future editorial implementation; does not publish or automatically validate factual claims.
decision_semantics.needs_revision: Owner suggests a change; notes provide direction.
decision_semantics.rejected: Decline this suggestion, not necessarily its underlying diagnosis.

items.title: Give the reader an actionable reward sooner
items.section: Article-wide
items.proposal:
Move “Practicing Community Can Start Now” and its strongest “Practice Before Committing” passages directly after the four-part model. The current text moves from the theory to a multi-part Zapatista history, then a long psychedelics discussion, before telling the ordinary reader how to begin without land. A reader who does not want to take medicine should not have to traverse that material to find the invitation they can act on this week.

Keep the practical suggestion—weekly meals, a two-person listening exchange, shared tools or childcare, then a real disagreement—near the front. Later membership policy can build on that experience.
items.note: Approve the direction, then review linked samples and section decisions separately.

items.title: Decide where the essay ends and a field manual begins
items.section: Article-wide
items.proposal:
In the same flow as the family story, the article supplies detailed protocols for admission reviews, children's allegations, psychiatry/medicine, technological dependence, federation records, shared money, expelled members and dissolution. Much of that matters. Not every reader needs the procedure during the first encounter with the vision.

Preferred test: one readable main essay, plus a clearly labeled companion/appendix for operational questions. This can live within one Substack post if desired, but the narrative should come first and the reference details should be visibly optional. A possible main-essay length of roughly 8,000–10,000 words is an editing experiment, not a quota or permission to cut unique material. The remainder can stay accessible as reference material. Alternatively, preserve the full length but give it a clear “essay / design notebook” boundary.

The appendix currently contains reading sources. It could also carry operational checklists—provided those are genuinely easy to locate. Do not hide safety instructions whose absence would change immediate decisions.
items.note: Approve the direction, then review linked samples and section decisions separately.

items.title: Make the two recurring arguments deliberate refrains, not fresh explanations
items.section: Article-wide
items.proposal:
The article teaches the inner/outer freedom distinction in the childhood retrospect, the “two ways” section, the four-part model, the reparenting passage, the Zapatista example, the jealousy section, and the closing. Keep the strongest definition once and let the other instances show how it plays out.

Likewise, accountability rather than charismatic dependency appears under spirituality, medicine, founderism, membership, children, federations, and leaving. Those appearances do not all duplicate one another: the stakes change. But several begin with another general explanation of why one person should not hold all the power. Keep the new evidence and new decision each time; use a short callback for the familiar premise.

Use the escuelita in three clear roles: the initial promise; the Zapatista model of teaching by living; the eventual daughter-project payoff. Avoid introducing its full definition from scratch elsewhere.

items.title: Reclaim narrative movement in the Zapatista and medicine blocks
items.section: Article-wide
items.proposal:
The muddy road, intimidating café visitor, basketball and direct encounter make the Zapatista material human. The precise institutional inventory, graduate-outcome provenance, and money qualifications can be trimmed or moved without losing the central authority and teaching lessons. Most importantly, the “Zap spirituality enigma” paragraph moves from an impression into unevidenced ideas about an Indigenous political movement’s drug practice. That is an evidentiary leap and a distracting detour, not a necessary defense of your own spiritual emphasis.

The medicine section similarly moves through five roles: “I'm mentioning medicine,” integration, benefits, risks, anti-guru philosophy and detailed precautions. Keep its uniquely relevant argument trusted relationships + meaningful follow-through + accountability + competent safeguards. The long disputed details about shamans, ritual aesthetics, and spirit attacks can be evaluated separately rather than allowed to displace the purpose of the section. No recommendation here authorizes deleting important medical screening or emergency-readiness content.

items.title: Put founder power, exit rights and children's outcomes close enough to test the dream
items.section: Article-wide
items.proposal:
The four founder questions are arguably the strongest piece of portable wisdom in the article. They come very late. Give them greater prominence soon after the model and first practical application, then use later chapters to show concrete consequences: deeds, criticism and complaints, children, privacy, and the actual resources needed to leave.

The grown children's final review is another excellent test. Its friend’s “treasure and a burden” account deserves breathing room. The lengthy defense of a specific vaccine worldview becomes a separate controversy just when the article wants to talk about how children judge the freedom they inherited. If the worldview belongs, place it as an explicit example of values that communities must settle beforehand, with independently verified claims; it need not monopolize the child-review transition.

items.title: Proposed eight-phase reader order
items.section: Article-wide
items.proposal:
1 — How I came to this question: Father’s film and family story, especially Love Israel / East Wind / Zendik — Establish stakes through lived experience.
2 — Why the experiments failed: Two ways communities die; the brief Freeloader Problem — Name the inner/outer gap and the material problem.
3 — What I want to try: Four pl/ork functions; inner and relational practice — Give a legible model before technical conditions.
4 — Begin without buying land: “Practicing Community Can Start Now,” “Practice group of whom?,” “Practice Before Committing” — Give readers something they could actually do.
5 — Learning to spread it: Zapatista visit, accountable leadership, 2023 revisions, escuelita, experiments before splitting — Demonstrate teaching by living without presenting it as a reproducible formula.
6 — The tests no utopia gets to skip: Founderism and four questions, children’s review, jealousy, membership, shared money, leaving rights, essential safeguards — Show what would keep this from becoming another prison or guru project.
7 — The optional tools and contested boundaries: Medicine, technosphere, detailed membership/safeguarding/health and governance specifications — Let interested readers go deep without making them prerequisites to following the main essay.
8 — Reality and continuation: Sénégal's hospitality and its limits, Black Tax, federation/daughter projects, your father’s film — End in an inhabited world rather than an organizational flowchart.

No paragraph is automatically removed; review the moves against each section’s function and media placement.
items.note: A trial structure only; may be revised without rejecting the underlying diagnosis.

items.title: Make the stewardship problem visible
items.section: Communes Are Hot Again 🔥 / The Freeloader Problem
items.proposal: Moves the concept into the pictured consequence, while preserving the responsibility and informal-power arguments. The hammock image is already yours; “picture” keeps it illustrative rather than a newly claimed specific incident.
items.source_quote:
I’d say the comment above is more true of the big socialism experiments than small communes, but I still take it seriously, because some people really would rather let somebody else take responsibility. Sometimes you see the same three people whoi end up doing all the maintenance, while everybody else talks about freedom while lounging around in their hammocks. And then unofficial leaders start gaining power just based on their indispensibility.

Communal ownership entails folks taking on visible and named stewardship duties. It requires knowing what to do if someone is leeching off the group and how to deal with it. It requires developing healthier forms of relationships. No, taking away the idea of a boss does not make everyone less passive, selfish, thieving, nor suddenly unlearning learned helplessness.
items.proposed_text: Picture three people doing all the maintenance while everyone else lounges in hammocks discussing freedom. Eventually those three are indispensable, and without anyone electing them, they’ve got real power. Getting rid of bosses doesn’t automatically make everybody responsible. If the land and tools belong to everyone, somebody still has to agree to look after them—and there has to be a way to deal with people who won’t.

items.title: Make the no-shaman point without another essay
items.section: The Medicine Part - Yes, I’m Naming It / No Special Shamans
items.proposal: Preserves expertise, non-guru principle and concrete safeguards. The dropped examples about allegedly harmful shamans and ritual aesthetics are not adjudicated here; retain in research notes or restore only after a relevance/source decision.
items.source_quote:
Traditional lineages usually disagree with me on this, and many ayahuasca tribes and Bwiti iboga communities believe the medicine should stay under trained lineage authority. I respect what those traditions have preserved, and I’ve learned some “dos & don’t dos” from their sensible practices and less sensible practices. For example, although I do highly value loving kindness meditation , inner child reparenting , and nibbana meditation before ceremony, during, and at all times, I notice a lot of people want their ceremony to look and feel like some kind of abstract mix of indigenous rituals & props to make it feel more authentic and sacred than their everyday life. I understand the benefit of setting aside one time and place for sacred experiences (the book, “God is Red” comes to mind), although the shadow side to that is making the spiritual seem like another world apart from your regular life, which is sort of opposite to integration.

And while I do think it’s valuable to have someone highly experienced in navigating the spirit worlds who is able to sense where you are in those and guide you, I also wouldn’t trust many of these shamans to guide me, considering it’s common to find that even the ones who can heal people very well may still be happy to send evil spirits to kill someone, if that hit job is lucrative. I also don’t trust their medical intuition in general, considering the Huni Kuin shamans are famous for claiming that all other ayahuasca shamans are giving people cancer by using the knotted B. caapi vine (since the knots remind them of tumors). They’re right though that modern folk do very often decide they’re ready to lead ceremonies long before they’re really trained and prepared. I’m sure I could still learn a lot from those traditions, and they will continue to develop their understandings as well.
items.proposed_text: I respect the experience preserved by traditional medicine lineages, and I’ve learned from some of their practices. I also don’t want one person becoming the unquestionable authority over everyone else’s spiritual life. A community might have people with much more experience than others, but experience shouldn’t put anyone beyond questions or accountability. Nor does rejecting a guru make amateurs competent: medical screening, sober care and emergency plans still matter.

items.source_quote:
The founder(s) end(s) up with real influence, and pretending they don’t just makes that influence harder to look at. When that power fails to get distributed as the conditions ripen for that, it’s called founderism, which is a fledgling form of what can become a subtle dictatorship.

I’ve seen founderism in many communes that I’ve visited, and I can see it playing out if I were to be a founder as well. I’ve got all these proposals and visions here in my guides, and so it would be very easy for me to become the person who decides whether or not everyone else “understood” them correctly, even while I wish to remain humble and open to the input of all involved.

That’s why the four questions below matter even if the founder is sincere.

items.title: Make a federation a possibility, not an organizational memorandum
items.section: From One Community to a Movement
items.proposal: Preserves the federation’s mutual-aid and anti-centralization function. Exact structures, PEACH governance, budget obligations and case ledgers should remain available in companion reference material if moved.
items.source_quote:
The problem of how these communities stay connected does eventually need to be solved somehow, if the idea is for them to spread without building another state. It should be solved in a way that allows help between communities and the movement of people and knowledge, and also keeps the differences alive, so communities can keep learning from one another. And communities already do have federations which provide some degrees of assistance in training people, seeding new projects, logging experiences and lessons, and so forth.

The Federation of Egalitarian Communities (FEC) says it’s rebuilding, and that’s a good warning. It takes work to run a federation. Delegates. Records. Compliance. Coordinating resources. Holding meetings. Succession. Whatever dispute function it actually takes on. These things all take up labor and material capacity before any local crisis has eaten into both. If the legal or economic environment requires money, the federation also needs to have a cash budget for dealing with it. But the work of federation doesn’t have to be done by a single entity. Two communities might want to be closely linked as friends, and that doesn’t stop both of them from also being part of a general federation. There can also be local clusters, or single-function institutions like the FEC’s PEACH health pool , which isn’t currently governed by the FEC delegates.
items.proposed_text: If one community teaches people how to build another, the new ones will eventually need ways to help each other without creating a government above them. Maybe two neighboring communities share tools or childcare. Maybe several run a health pool or help a new group find land. Some federations already try versions of this, and the hard part is easy to underestimate: somebody still has to do the meetings, records and follow-through. I’d rather those jobs be shared than put one new headquarters in charge.

items.title: Stop the dissolution inventory after the reader understands
items.section: Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution / When the Community Dissolves
items.proposal: The original lists more critical functions—records, education, animals, contact, transport and obligations. Those must be carried into a real dissolution checklist if this shorter narrative version is adopted.
items.source_quote: If the community dissolves, what happens to the land and any outside debts? What about its buildings, equipment, common stores or funds? What happens to each member’s agreed rights? More immediately, who is responsible for ensuring that everyone has a place to live and food to eat? Who takes responsibility for making sure people get their medications and the other care they need? Who keeps childcare going, and makes sure the kids’ schooling carries on? Who takes responsibility for transportation, for the records, for family contact, for the animals, for making sure land obligations are met, and for any unresolved claims? That’s a lot of loose ends!
items.proposed_text: Suppose the community dissolves. The land and debts have to be settled, but people still need meals, medication, housing and childcare the next morning. Who has agreed to keep those going while everything else is being untangled? If you haven’t worked that out, the right to walk away might be only a right on paper.

items.title: Use Senegal as a lived test of the thesis
items.section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
items.proposal: This combines several original thoughts without adding a claim about all Senegalese or Africans. It leaves the subsequent examples about exclusion and obligations to supply specific complications. Residency tips and tourism facts could live elsewhere.
items.source_quote:
I live in Sénégal, where “intentional community” often sounds like a strange Western phrase. People here are like, “Don’t human beings already do that?”

Westerners often start out isolated and try to rebuild a tribe. A lot of Africans start out with a communal life they inherited, and watch parts of it fall apart. Kind of the opposite problem. And urban Africans who get interested in intentional community might come to it feeling alienated from both the city and the tradition they left. So the issue is global now, not just a “first world problem.”

In the villages and families I’ve spent time around, so much is taken care of by the extended family and the local memory, alongside the formal systems. Whether it’s land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc, etc. I’d probably not sell any tickets if I held a workshop called, “Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging.” 😅

Oh, and a practical note: getting my residency in Sénégal was pretty cheap and straightforward. French and Wolof matter a lot more than English. And the country’s famous ideal of Teranga (hospitality) is real in my life. I’m staying in a friend’s family’s house, and they won’t let me pay rent! Of course that Teranga is part and parcel of the whole culture of watchfulness, witchcraft, social conservatism, bureaucracy and all the usual complications of a real society and country.
items.proposed_text: Living in Sénégal has made the phrase “intentional community” sound a little strange to me. In the families I’ve spent time with, sharing food, space and obligations isn’t a new social experiment. I’m living with a friend’s family now, and they won’t even let me pay rent. That kind of hospitality has real costs and complications, too. Some people inherit a communal life and watch it weaken; others are trying to rebuild one from scratch. Neither problem is solved by a pretty slogan about belonging.

items.title: End on the test, not another qualification
items.section: A Hope For Humanity
items.proposal: A possible alternative closing, not an approved replacement. It keeps the documentary, spread-by-learning, founder test, nonrecruitment and Uncle Joe joke. If the existing bolder joke is important, keep it; the core editorial issue is giving the essay an earned landing.
items.source_quote:
Decades after the Bruderhof shaped my father, I’m publishing the film he made, and writing this.

Maybe some of you will build something useful from this. Maybe that community will teach someone else, who’ll build another. Passing it on doesn’t need one institution or one founder. And there doesn’t have to be one official version of it, either.

I am not currently recruiting anyone or founding a community, which makes it easier for me to write an article like this, since I’m not trying to get you onto my land. I do plan to find some land, and people may naturally end up living around me. All of the warnings in this article apply to me, too. Based on the folks who’ve so far expressed interest, I’m planning to call my commune, “Uncle Joe’s Crazy Farm.” 🤪 Hopefully not gonna be another Trungpa Rinpoche cult.
items.proposed_text: My father spent years asking where utopia was. I don’t think there’s one perfect piece of land waiting for us. I’d be happier to see a place where people learn to care for one another, question the founder, leave freely and, if they want, start something else. I’m not recruiting anybody now, though I hope to find land someday. And if Uncle Joe’s Crazy Farm actually happens, I hope everybody remembers the four questions before they decide to follow Uncle Joe.
